power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Two major criticisms of attention research are: 1) verbal theories lack the specificity to make falsifiable predictions about how the various mechanisms of attention operate; and 2) the term "attention" is frequently ascribed to conceptually similar phenomena despite dissociable neural underpinnings.

The field of model-based cognitive neuroscience is well-positioned to address (1) through mathematical formalization of hypothesized processes, but may perpetuate (2) insofar as similar algorithms and parameters may recur across modeling traditions without necessarily drawing upon a shared neuro-mechanistic basis.

This review provides a functionfirst organization of the algorithms that have been hypothesized to implement or give rise to "attention" at various levels of processing: perception, decision-making, and learning.
We ground mathematically-formalized processes in the performance-relevant objectives they serve and the processing constraints that limit them.
In doing so, we provide a road map of the broader computational-level solutions that "attention" mechanisms have been invoked to provide.

Despite William James's often-quoted, pre-theoretical notion that "Everyone knows what attention is," (James, 1890, p. 403), efforts to empirically define, measure, and explain attention have produced considerable controversy.

text.text: The need to revise the concept of unitary attention was powerfully captured by Alan Allport:

Even a brief survey of the heterogeneity and functional separability of different components of spatial and nonspatial attentional control prompts the conclusion that, qua causal mechanism, there can be no such thing as attention.
There is no one uniform computational function or mental operation (in general no one causal mechanism) to which all so-called attentional phenomena can be attributed. (Allport, 1993, p. 203).

text.text: Modern perspectives thus accommodate mechanistic disunity by characterizing "attention" as a general term for processes that prioritize information for ongoing thought and action (Wu, 2011; Watzl, 2011; Wu, 2024; Smithies, 2011; Koralus, 2014).

text.text: When attention is no longer treated as a single quantity or explanatory operation, new research questions emerge: what are the various mechanisms through which information is prioritized, and what factors determine which mechanisms are engaged?
This paper provides a state-of-the-field review of how model-based cognitive neuroscience has addressed these questions.

Given its emphasis on mathematical formalization, we suggest that this subfield is particularly well-suited to understanding "attention" as many mechanisms that may be instantiated differently depending on the goal and the neural systems involved (Palmeri et al., 2015; Turner et al., 2017; Kriegeskorte & Douglas, 2018; Forstmann & Turner, 2024).

text.text: Unlike verbal theories in which "attention" is presented as metaphors (Di Lollo, 2018) or retrofit latent causes of observed effects (B. Anderson, 2011), there is less room for ambiguity when hypotheses must be mathematically specified.

text.text: Accordingly, model-based cognitive neuroscience approaches involve expressing process-level hypotheses as systems of equations, and comparing predictions against against behavioral and neurophysiological data (e.g., from human, non-human primate, or other animal participants).
In many cases, fitting and comparing models based on how well they account for both behavioral outputs and process-level data provides the specificity to adjudicate among competing accounts.

While many existing reviews helpfully classify attentional phenomena into subtypes for targeted study (e.g., Klein, 2022; Posner & Petersen, 1990; Corbetta & Shulman, 2002), this review examines how model-based cognitive neuroscience approaches have operationalized "attention" in terms of neural mechanisms.

text.text: Although model-based cognitive neuroscience may offer valuable explanatory power, formal precision does not necessarily equate to a generalizable understanding of how the brain works.

This literature is often siloed according to specific modeling traditions, such that models that operate at the timescales relevant to perception, decision-making, and learning invoke overlapping constructs (i.e., as parameters) without intending to imply a shared neural mechanism (Kvam & Alaukik, 2026).

text.text: Attentional mechanisms of interest, such as competitive inhibition and multiplicative gain, may therefore recur across models of individual tasks while drawing upon different neural processes and networks.

Mathematical formalization may solve the problem of conceptual overreach, but a proliferation of task-specific mechanisms may 'miss the forest for the trees' by obscuring general principles for how and why information is prioritized.
To address this, the current review provides a high-level function-first organization of the mechanisms hypothesized in model-based cognitive neuroscience to comprise-or give rise to-attention.

When many implementations are considered together, a shared structure becomes visible: the processing domain (i.e., perception, decision-making, learning) comprises a problem space with an objective and constraints, and "attention" constitutes a set of solutions for navigating the space effectively.

As summarized by Table 1, objectives refer to desired performance outcomes and constraints refer to the resource, capacity, and informational factors that limit the system's ability to achieve those outcomes (Lieder & Griffiths, 2019).

text.text: To conduct the present structured narrative review, we identified articles that fit the following a priori inclusion criteria: 1) mechanisms of attention were a primary theoretical focus; 2) a computational model was fit to observed output; and 3) process-level neurophysiological or neuroanatomical data informed or constrained model predictions (functional magnetic resonance imaging, fMRI; electroencephalography, EEG; single-unit recording; eye-tracking; tissue volume).
A total of 64 articles were identified.

We first organized the identified papers according to the recurring processing domains of perception and encoding, comparing and evaluating decision evidence, and learning, which reflect the principal contexts in which model-based cognitive neuroscience has formalized attentional mechanisms.
We emphasize that while these domains provide a useful organizing structure for this literature, they are not intended to accommodate all models that exist.

Models that focus on emotion (Ong et al., 2020), memory retrieval (Vasishth et al., 2019), and language (Goldstein et al., 2022) that do not explicitly specify a mechanistic role for attentionor do not describe how attentional phenomena emergeare not discussed here.

Domains reflect recurring contexts in which the included models were applied, and each is characterized by an overarching objective and biological or processing constraints.

Mechanisms described as "attention" are grouped according to the computational-level solutions they provide for navigating these tradeoffs, and each solution may encompass multiple alternative algorithmic specifications or neural implementations.

Within each dedicated solution subsection, we review papers that algorithmically formalize the given solution, and explicate how it is physically implemented by neural systems.

Ultimately, this function-first organizing structure provides an accessible entry point into an otherwise fragmented literature, allowing researchers to start with a functional hypothesis and identify relevant processlevel modeling work.
Visual perception and encoding transform low-level sensory inputs into internal representations that support accurate inference and adaptive action (e.g., Creem-Regehr & Kunz, 2010).

text.text: Maintaining high-fidelity representations across all sensory inputs, however, is fundamentally bounded by the metabolic costs of neural firing (i.e., glucose and oxygen; Niven & Laughlin, 2008; Wong-Riley, 2010) and limits on the temporal persistence and capacity of visual processing (Enns & Di Lollo, 1997; Di Lollo et al., 2000).

text.text: Mecha-nisms operationalized as "attention" address these biological and processing limits through three recurring functional solutions: by selectively prioritizing unpredicted sensory inputs over predictable ones (Solution 1.1), by focusing perceptual processing toward goal-relevant features or locations rather than distributing resources uniformly across sensory space (Solution 1.2), and by gating which sensory inputs enter downstream, capacity-limited systems (Solution 1.3).
A central computational pressure in perceptual systems is the need to accurately represent sensory input while minimizing energy cost.
Early single-cell recordings in the visual cortex established that neurons exhibit selective tuning for local stimulus properties within receptive fields (Hubel & Wiesel, 1965 , 1968).

text.text: However, subsequent work demonstrated that firing in the presence of a preferred input is suppressed when matching stimulus features are simultaneously represented by surrounding neurons (Allman et al., 1985).

text.text: Computational modeling work leveraged these extraclassical surround effects to formalize a core optimization strategy in perception: reduction of prediction-redundant processing.
In natural environments, a large proportion of visual information is redundant across space and time.
Static background elements like the sky and ground, for example, remain largely unchanged from one moment to the next.

Constant transmission of raw, fully predictable sensory input would consume an untenable amount of metabolic energy, and deplete the resources available to process novel or dynamic objects that are of more immediate concern to the organism's survival.

Sensory architectures can therefore balance representational accuracy with resource efficiency by making and evaluating predictions, and using prediction error as a signal to selectively propagate information up the cortical hierarchy.

Predictive coding models accomplish this by representing the visual system as a neural network with bottom-up and top-down connections (Rao & Ballard, 1999; Mumford, 1992; Friston, 2005; McClelland & Rumelhart, 1981).
text.formatted: Predictive coding models accomplish this by representing the visual system as a neural network with bottom-up and top-down connections <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">(Rao & Ballard, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Mumford, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Friston, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">McClelland & Rumelhart, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: When processing sensory input, these models instantiate the following properties 1) superordinate layers (e.g., V2 relative to V1) learn statistical regularities across multiple images as they are processed over time; 2) top-down connections communicate predicted activation patterns to subordinate layers; 3) bottom-up connections communicate how reality deviated from the prediction, rather than a comprehensive impression of reality itself; and 4) superordinate layers update predictions based on error signals received from subordinate layers.
The hypothesized system, in other words, simultaneously optimizes for the goals of making accurate predictions and minimizing redundant input signal.

Simulations of predictive coding models have replicated several observed properties of neuronal populations in the visual cortex, including the aforementioned suppression effect when a neuron's preferred input extends beyond its receptive field.
Selectivity emerges naturally from predictive coding architectures, insofar as inputs that deviate from expectation receive privileged processing relative to inputs that match expectation.

In the related specification provided by biased competition models, attention is explicitly described as the selectivity that results from top-down biases influencing which inputs within the receptive field receive enhanced processing (Desimone & Duncan, 1995).

text.text: To function effectively, the perceptual system cannot unilaterally ignore well-predicted information.
Instead, it must flexibly adapt which inputs are selected for additional processing according to behavioral goals.
A traffic light may remain statically red for several moments, yet it requires continuous monitoring so that the observer is prepared to react when it turns green.

At the level of the neuron, mechanisms that suppress processing of predicted inputs may, at times, conflict with top-down attention processes that prioritize task-relevant inputs (Corbetta et al., 1990; Brefczynski & DeYoe, 1999).

text.text: Two counterbalanced cue types were provided at the outset of each block: 1) a prediction cue accurately informed participants whether stimuli were more likely to appear in the left or right hemifield; 2) a task-based cue instructed participants to only respond to stimuli that appeared in either the left or the right hemifield.

Fits of a Bayesian causal model to connectivity data showed that while the nodes of visual cortex self-inhibit at baseline, task-relevant prioritization overrode this state and enhanced the forward drive of sensory information through the early visual cortical hierarchy (V1 to V2 and V3).
While these interactions shape low-level feature representation in early visual areas, predictive coding principles also extend to higher, category-selective levels of the visual hierarchy.

Activity in the fusiform face area (FFA), for example, has been linked to visual processing of faces (Kanwisher et al., 1997). Egner et al. (2010) contrasted three possibilities regarding the role of prediction in the FFA, using a task where faces and houses were preceded by colored frames that were probabilistically predictive of category.

(2010)</ref> contrasted three possibilities regarding the role of prediction in the FFA, using a task where faces and houses were preceded by colored frames that were probabilistically predictive of category.

text.text: First, if FFA activity primarily reflects bottom-up category information, faces should elicit greater activation than houses regardless of expectation.
Second, predictive cues could recruit topdown attention, such that expecting a face amplifies FFA response when a face is subsequently presented.
Third, under predictive coding, FFA activity should reflect both the expectation of a face and the prediction error generated when a house is expected but a face is presented.
FFA activation was best explained by predictive coding without additional mechanisms for expectation-based enhancement.

Taken together, these findings demonstrate that dissociable mechanisms of prediction error and task-relevant prioritization can enhance processing of both low-level sensory features and high-level category features.
As foregrounded in the previous section, perceptual systems must prioritize sensory signals that align with current task goals in addition to reducing predictive redundancy.

These results suggest that conditions of focused (as opposed to divided) attention amplify discriminability via multiplicative sensory gain in the earliest stages of perceptual encoding, prior to the pooling of neuronal responses into a decision-relevant readout.
A critical theoretical gap in accounts of perceptual enhancement concerns how goal-relevant objects are selected for enhancement in the first place.

Located within the prefrontal cortex (PFC), the FEF functions as a priority map that integrates salience-driven and goal-driven signals to identify saccade targets (Schall et al., 1995; Itti & Koch, 2000; Murthy et al., 2001; Lowe & Schall, 2018).

The previous subsections highlighted several examples in which task-based goals (via top-down projections) were hypothesized to dictate which sensory inputs were prioritized for perceptual processing.
The relevant algorithms thus largely focused on optimizing discriminability and performance.
Other model-based accounts, such as those discussed here, are additionally considerate of capacity constraints when specifying mechanisms that would support overall performance.

A recurring theme is that capacity bottlenecks are assumed to apply to higher-level processes (e.g., memory; Cowan, 2001), and "attentional" mechanisms applied during early perception are a means to gate access.

text.text: The limits of memory consolidation become particularly clear in rapid serial visual presentation tasks that give rise to the attentional blink-the robust failure to detect a second visual target (T2) when it appears within 500 ms of a first (T1; Broadbent & Broadbent, 1987; Raymond et al., 1992; Kawahara et al., 2001).

The resulting temporal bottleneck was initially formalized as a consequence of transient neuromodulatory dynamics within the locus coeruleus-norepinephrine (LC-NE) system (Nieuwenhuis, Gilzenrat, et al., 2005; Nieuwenhuis, Aston-Jones, & Cohen, 2005; Usher et al., 1999).

text.text: As implemented in these connectionist frameworks, sensory inputs are multiplicatively scaled by "attention" resulting from LC-NE release.

Because the LC undergoes a brief refractory period following stimulus-driven NE release (e.g., when T1 is presented), subsequent inputs arriving during this recovery window fail to receive attentional scaling.

This biocomputational account directly links the behavioral timecourse of the attentional blink to neurophysiological markers of LC-NE activity, including single-unit firing in non-human primates, P3 event-related potential (ERP) amplitudes, and task-evoked pupil dilation (Nieuwenhuis, Gilzenrat, et al., 2005; Sergent et al., 2005; Jepma & Nieuwenhuis, 2011).

text.text: The accounts discussed here demonstrate that while all of these models address the same attentional phenomenon, they formalize "attention" and its neural implementations in fundamentally distinct ways.

Gated propagation of sensory input to memory may be an unintended consequence of attention-mediated perceptual encoding (Nieuwenhuis, Gilzenrat, et al., 2005), or it may be a purposeful means of segmenting memory traces via top-down attention (Wyble et al., 2009), or it may emerge from interactions between control and memory processes that do not necessitate an additional "attention" mechanism at all (van Vugt, 2014).

text.text: Considering these perspectives together highlights how computational modeling allows us to dissociate the behavioral signatures of a temporal limit from the diverse mechanical routes that plausibly produce it.

While these accounts arguably implement the same computational-level solution for forming useful memory representations under processing constraints, the most theoretically meaningful distinctions lie at the level of algorithms and their neural implementations.
Once information is available to guide behavior, it must be evaluated relative to current goals, stored knowledge, and competing alternatives in order to select an appropriate action.
Evidence accumulation models (EAMs) provide a foundational framework for how organisms process competing options over time and make decisions (Boag et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Evidence accumulation models (EAMs) provide a foundational framework for how organisms process competing options over time and make decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Boag et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In these models, the observer is thought to collect and evaluate evidence for each available option over time in reference to a criterion, which may take the form of a sensory, memorybased, or value-based signal depending on the task.
Drift rate parameters represent the quality of evidence stemming from each option and the threshold or boundary separation parameter represents a level of evidence needed for a choice to be made.

Importantly, the evidence accumulation process is "noisy," such that a simple comparison of drift rates does not perfectly explain choice; an incorrect or less valuable option may be spuriously selected.
The evidence accumulation framework naturally formalizes a cost-benefit tradeoff.

Because evidence is noisy and time is costly, the cognitive system must balance competing objectives: integrating information long enough to sup-port accurate selection, while minimizing the costs of continued deliberation and delayed action.

The threshold specifically manages this trade-off between speed and accuracy, with higher thresholds generating slower response times (RTs) and choices less susceptible to spurious error (Heitz, 2014).
text.formatted: The threshold specifically manages this trade-off between speed and accuracy, with higher thresholds generating slower response times (RTs) and choices less susceptible to spurious error <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Heitz, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Time minimization can reflect strict environmental constraints or an observer's preference, both of which pressure the system to balance deliberation against commitment to a choice.

Evidence accumulation also appears to be cognitively effortful, as indexed by increased BOLD response in frontal and sensorimotor regions during difficult choices and multi-attribute integration (T. Liu & Pleskac, 2011; Lee & Daunizeau, 2021).

text.text: Within this framework, studies in model-based cognitive neuroscience conceptualize various ways in which "attention" manages this tradeoff, including algorithms that dynamically regulate evidence quality and decision policy as task demands change (Solution 2.1), regulate comparisons between options over time (Solution 2.2), and selectively prioritize certain attributes within multidimensional comparisons (Solution 2.3).

Whereas perceptual accounts of so-called "attentional" mechanisms (Section 1) describe how and why particular sensory inputs are selected for processing and admittance into internal representations, decision-making accounts have a somewhat different overarching focus and address different questions.
The relevant output in the latter accounts is an action-relevant signal-what to do with an input-rather than an encoded trace of the input itself.

While some algorithms may appear to recur across perception and decisionmaking (e.g., multiplicative gain; competitive inhibition and enhancement), this review is organized to highlight the importance of system-level objectives and constraints when drawing functional interpretations.
A neural system optimizing for representational fidelity may produce a different output than one optimizing for a correct overt decision, despite involving overlapping transformations.
Perceptual decision-making requires sensory information to be converted into task-relevant decision evidence, which is then evaluated relative to a threshold.

Because classical EAMs such as the standard diffusion decision model (DDM; Ratcliff, 1978) assume a relatively predictable trajectory for this transformation across trials, questions have emerged about the extent to which top-down adjustments to increase accuracy or conserve resources are possible, and how those adjustments might be implemented.

text.text: Real-world perceptual decision-making tasks, like detecting and reacting to forthcoming curves in the road when driving in heavy fog, present distinct computational challenges: extracting high-fidelity signal from noisy sensory input and preserving accumulated evidence over time against decay, distraction, or capacity bottlenecks.

Rather than beginning with perceptual encoding, however, value-based decisions are assumed to begin with the activation of existing, complex internal representations of each option.

text.text: Likewise, the magnitude of aDDM's implementation of attentional bias depends on peripheral visibility: masking unfixated options approximately doubles the bias induced by differential gaze, suggesting that peripheral vision normally permits partial processing of unattended alternatives (Eum et al., 2023).

text.text: Taken together, these findings characterize gaze as a flexible weighting mechanism whose algorithmic form is relatively stable, but whose influence on evidence accumulation depends on an option's current perceived alignment with a task-based goal (e.g., choose the subjectively-valued "best" option; choose the objectively correct option) relative to other alternatives.

By incorporating observed fixation patterns directly into the accumulation process, aDDM successfully accounts for trial-level choice-RT properties and idiosyncrasies that are not well-captured by noisy accumulation alone.

Relative to previously-discussed perception models whose mechanisms either give rise to attentional phenomena or predict which stimuli will be fixated, however, aDDM is agnostic to the saccade-generating process itself.

It is therefore well-suited for investigating the impact of hypothesized attention mechanisms on decision outcomes, but does not explain when and why gaze shifts occur during the decision-making process.
The aDDM's single-accumulator architecture is specifically suited to binary choice scenarios.

Binary choice, however, provides limited leverage for determining what happens to evidence associated with unfixated optionsstrengthening one alternative and weakening its sole competitor have equivalent consequences for relative preference.

Investigations of multi-alternative choice provide the opportunity to disentangle these processes: models can instantiate competing hypotheses about how gaze alters evidence for a fixated option and how evidence associated with unfixated alternatives is maintained, lost, or actively suppressed.

Robust context effects in multi-alternative choice provide a fascinating set of test cases whereby, for example, the presence of an undesirable third option systematically shifts preference between the remaining alternatives, despite rarely being chosen itself (Huber et al., 1982; Simonson, 1989).
text.formatted: Robust context effects in multi-alternative choice provide a fascinating set of test cases whereby, for example, the presence of an undesirable third option systematically shifts preference between the remaining alternatives, despite rarely being chosen itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Huber et al., 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b160">Simonson, 1989)</ref>.

text.text: Computational accounts capture these context effects using attention implemented as weights that scale pairwise option comparisons (Roe et al., 2001; Trueblood et al., 2014; Noguchi & Stewart, 2014; Turner et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Computational accounts capture these context effects using attention implemented as weights that scale pairwise option comparisons <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">(Roe et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b181">Trueblood et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">Noguchi & Stewart, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">Turner et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, eye-tracking evidence demonstrates that gaze allocation is itself dynamically shaped by option value: higher-valued alternatives increasingly attract visual sampling as the trial unfolds.

An extended aDDM captured these dynamics by allowing accumulated evidence to influence subsequent fixation probabilities, thereby introducing reciprocal interactions between gaze and evidence accumulation (Gluth et al., 2020).
text.formatted: An extended aDDM captured these dynamics by allowing accumulated evidence to influence subsequent fixation probabilities, thereby introducing reciprocal interactions between gaze and evidence accumulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Gluth et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Model comparisons have favored accounts where gaze controls evidence accumulation, and evidence leaks away from unfixated options rather than being subject to lateral inhibition (Glickman et al., 2019; Molter et al., 2022).

text.text: Some individual differences have been identified, however, such that both leak and lateral inhibition are needed to account for data from individuals who exhibit extreme context effects (Molter et al., 2022).

text.text: While gaze-mediated gain control accelerates deliberation, it does not universally optimize choice accuracy.

Indeed, individuals with lower numeracy show greater distortion of the evidence favoring unfixated alternatives, and simulations have suggested that gaze-mediated evidence accumulation can degrade choice quality when internal value representations are poorly calibrated (Zilker, 2024).
text.formatted: Indeed, individuals with lower numeracy show greater distortion of the evidence favoring unfixated alternatives, and simulations have suggested that gaze-mediated evidence accumulation can degrade choice quality when internal value representations are poorly calibrated <ref type="bibr" target="#b207">(Zilker, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: If "attention" in decision frameworks can reduce decision quality, one wonders what objective it serves.
One hypothesis is that participants seek to maximize reward rate, rather than overall value.
Attentional biases via gaze may shorten decision time by amplifying value, which may be a sufficient benefit for the system to overcome an occasional sacrifice to accuracy (Zilker, 2022).
text.formatted: Attentional biases via gaze may shorten decision time by amplifying value, which may be a sufficient benefit for the system to overcome an occasional sacrifice to accuracy <ref type="bibr" target="#b206">(Zilker, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, shifting gaze toward uncertain options may reflect an effort-confidence trade-off, where visual sampling may be upregulated to satisfy internal confi-dence thresholds rather than objective expected value (Lee & Daunizeau, 2021; Brus et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Alternatively, shifting gaze toward uncertain options may reflect an effort-confidence trade-off, where visual sampling may be upregulated to satisfy internal confi-dence thresholds rather than objective expected value <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">(Lee & Daunizeau, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Brus et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Characterizing the precise objective functions that govern these sampling policies remains a key frontier for unifying computational models of visual search and value-based choice.
While standard frameworks simplify decision-making by collapsing subjective value into a unidimensional quantity, real-world alternatives are inherently multidimensional.
The subjective value of a food item is a composite of taste, healthiness, price, and visual appeal.
Likewise, choosing between gambles in a risky choice task is thought to involve weighted comparisons of potential payoff, loss magnitude, and outcome probability (Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993).
text.formatted: Likewise, choosing between gambles in a risky choice task is thought to involve weighted comparisons of potential payoff, loss magnitude, and outcome probability <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Busemeyer & Townsend, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: In computational accounts of how attribute-wise information is combined into a decision-relevant signal, the relative influence of each attribute on choice is formalized as an "attention weight."
Estimating these weights from choice patterns has revealed that contextual demands and task goals can dynamically shift which specific attributes are prioritized (Turner et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Estimating these weights from choice patterns has revealed that contextual demands and task goals can dynamically shift which specific attributes are prioritized <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">(Turner et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Identifying which attributes individuals prioritize further provides important information about the objective they are personally seeking to optimize (Fisher, 2017).
text.formatted: Identifying which attributes individuals prioritize further provides important information about the objective they are personally seeking to optimize <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Fisher, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: A central computational problem in multi-attribute choice is determining how multidimensional feature inputs across multiple alternatives are transformed into a decision variable.

In principle, information can be integrated in two ways: within-option integration, where an option's attributes are first combined into a holistic subjective value before being compared to other alternatives; or within-attribute integration, where options are compared one attribute at a time and these attribute-wise contrasts are aggregated.
Gaze-informed EAM frameworks have provided a means to pit these competing integration accounts directly against one another.
Interestingly, model comparisons initially appeared to show that attribute integration and comparison occurs differently in different choice contexts.
In risky choice where each alternative has attributes for potential reward and win probability, the results favor within-option integration (Glickman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In risky choice where each alternative has attributes for potential reward and win probability, the results favor within-option integration <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Glickman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In intertemporal choice where each alternative has attributes for potential reward and a delay duration, by contrast, the results favor within-attribute integration (Amasino et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In intertemporal choice where each alternative has attributes for potential reward and a delay duration, by contrast, the results favor within-attribute integration <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Amasino et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, these accounts can be reconciled by allowing the integration strategy itself to be dynamically determined by relative attribute importance.

Extending the aDDM to accommodate separate attentional discounting parameters for unfixated options versus unfixated attributes demonstrated that within-option comparisons dominate when attribute weights are relatively balanced, whereas within-attribute comparisons take over when one feature dimension strongly outweighs another (Yang & Krajbich, 2022).
text.formatted: Extending the aDDM to accommodate separate attentional discounting parameters for unfixated options versus unfixated attributes demonstrated that within-option comparisons dominate when attribute weights are relatively balanced, whereas within-attribute comparisons take over when one feature dimension strongly outweighs another <ref type="bibr" target="#b205">(Yang & Krajbich, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Because potential reward often outweighs delay time in intertemporal choice, evaluation shifts toward withinattribute comparison; conversely, when potential reward and win probability carry more equal weight in risky choice, integration occurs within-option.

Feature-level salience further modulates this process: extreme attribute values (such as win probabilities near 0% or 100%) draw visual gaze and distort feature weights directly during accumulation (Zilker & Pachur, 2022).
text.formatted: Feature-level salience further modulates this process: extreme attribute values (such as win probabilities near 0% or 100%) draw visual gaze and distort feature weights directly during accumulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b208">(Zilker & Pachur, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest that evidence in multi-attribute choice is dynamically configured by the relative importance and salience of the available information, both of which can be instantiated through gaze-dependent weighting.
In multi-attribute decision models, attention weights reflect the subjective importance of an attribute when determining an option's value and deciding whether or not to select it.

"Attention weights" are similarly embedded in longstanding categorization models to account for different biases and strategies participants use to sort multidimensional object stimuli into categories (e.g., generalized context model, GCM; Nosofsky, 1986).
text.formatted: "Attention weights" are similarly embedded in longstanding categorization models to account for different biases and strategies participants use to sort multidimensional object stimuli into categories (e.g., generalized context model, GCM; <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Nosofsky, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: Categorization models formalize hypotheses about how internal category representations form over the course of experience and iterative feedback, with attention weights allowing some dimensions to be expanded and others to be compressed in psychological space.

Approaches that integrate neurophysiological measures and categorization models have provided a means to adjudicate between competing hypotheses about the structure of the internal representations that support categorization decisions.

A longstanding debate concerns whether these representations are organized around abstract category prototypes or preserve information about individual exemplars encountered during feedback-based learning (Minda & Smith, 2002; Nosofsky, 1986).
text.formatted: A longstanding debate concerns whether these representations are organized around abstract category prototypes or preserve information about individual exemplars encountered during feedback-based learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">(Minda & Smith, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">Nosofsky, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: The classic 5-4 category structure provides an especially useful opportunity for adjudication because prototype and exemplar models can produce similar categorization behavior while predicting different distributions of attention across stimulus dimensions (Medin & Shaffer, 1978).
text.formatted: The classic 5-4 category structure provides an especially useful opportunity for adjudication because prototype and exemplar models can produce similar categorization behavior while predicting different distributions of attention across stimulus dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">(Medin & Shaffer, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: Although no single physiological measure provides an agreed-upon ground truth against which to compare model-predicted "attention," eye movements and neural activity offer observable signals that can constrain otherwise behaviorally equivalent representational hypotheses.

In eye-tracking work, observed fixations across dimensions were more consistent with the attention weights estimated by the exemplar-based GCM than with a competing prototype account (Rehder & Hoffman, 2005b).
text.formatted: In eye-tracking work, observed fixations across dimensions were more consistent with the attention weights estimated by the exemplar-based GCM than with a competing prototype account <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">(Rehder & Hoffman, 2005b)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, latent representational similarity matrices generated by a fitted exemplar-based model corresponded more closely to multivoxel patterns of BOLD activity than those generated by a prototype model (Mack et al., 2013), with attention-weighted exemplar similarity reflected in lateral occipital, posterior parietal, and prefrontal cortices.
text.formatted: Similarly, latent representational similarity matrices generated by a fitted exemplar-based model corresponded more closely to multivoxel patterns of BOLD activity than those generated by a prototype model <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">(Mack et al., 2013)</ref>, with attention-weighted exemplar similarity reflected in lateral occipital, posterior parietal, and prefrontal cortices.

text.text: These convergent findings suggest that category representations maintain item-specific detail, with feature dimensions weighted dynamically during similarity comparison.
A critical question arising from these categorization frameworks is whether dimension-weighting reflects a dynamic decision-time policy or a structural property of stored memory traces.

If prioritization functioned merely as a latestage readout strategy, it would simply scale feature-level evidence during similarity evaluation without altering the fidelity of the underlying memory exemplar.

Indeed, eyetracking data indicates that weighting is highly strategic: dimensions containing unique, perfectly diagnostic features attract earlier fixations and consequently impose greater influence on decisions as determined by model-estimated "attention" (Z. Liu et al., 2015).

text.text: However, weighting effects do not appear to be confined to a late-stage decision-time readout process.

Rather than tracking activity in evaluative regions (e.g., ventromedial PFC; Bechara et al., 2000), GCMestimated dimension weights covary with feature decoding accuracy in the visual stream's category-selective occipitotemporal cortex (Braunlich & Love, 2019).

text.text: Model comparisons that used gaze during feature encoding and subsequent decision-making to constrain GCM attention weights additionally showed that accounting for partially encoded representations, in which unfixated dimensions may be absent from stored exemplars, was necessary to explain subsequent memory and categorization behavior (Weichart et al., 2024; Vance et al., 2025).

text.text: Consequently, "attention" parameters in GCM may reflect more than the observer's beliefs about which dimensions are most task-relevant; they can also reflect constraints imposed by selective encoding, whereby efficient prioritization during learning produces biased representations that shape subsequent generalization.

Defining a general objective for learning is a challenge in itself, and researchers across fields of psychology, artificial intelligence, and neuroscience have grappled with this question for decades (e.g. Klopf, 1972; Sutton & Barto, 1998).

text.text: For our purposes, we borrow from a rich tradition of reinforcement learning (RL) the idea of "a learning system that wants something, that adapts its behavior in order to maximize a special signal from its environment," (p. viii; Sutton & Barto, 1998).
text.formatted: For our purposes, we borrow from a rich tradition of reinforcement learning (RL) the idea of "a learning system that wants something, that adapts its behavior in order to maximize a special signal from its environment," (p. viii; <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">Sutton & Barto, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, the objective can be described as maximizing cumulative reward over time.
The agent's ability to maximize reward, particularly during early learning, is constrained by knowledge about actionoutcome contingencies within the environment.
These contingencies must typically be acquired through trial and error, requiring the agent to navigate environmental uncertainty and learn from limited feedback.

In classical RL terms, an optimal solution could be identified with a sufficiently rich representation of states, transitions, and rewards to simulate future trajectories and select actions that maximize expected long-run value.
This brute force approach, however, is intractable for real organisms.

The space of possible action sequences, exploration time, and complexity of value calculations quickly exceeds the feasible computational bandwidth of biological agents-a problem known as the curse of dimensionality (Bellman, 1957).
text.formatted: The space of possible action sequences, exploration time, and complexity of value calculations quickly exceeds the feasible computational bandwidth of biological agents-a problem known as the curse of dimensionality <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Bellman, 1957)</ref>.

text.text: In high-dimensional environments, the agent must further cope with the problem of credit assignment, or distinguishing between features that directly led to the reward, and those that were incidentally present (Minsky, 1961).
text.formatted: In high-dimensional environments, the agent must further cope with the problem of credit assignment, or distinguishing between features that directly led to the reward, and those that were incidentally present <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(Minsky, 1961)</ref>.

text.text: Attention in the context of learning thus comprises solutions that enable state abstraction (i.e., compressing a detailed state space) and selective credit assignment, allowing the agent to behave effectively despite incomplete knowledge of the environment's structure.
The ability to associate environmental cues with outcomes is essential for making accurate predictions, allowing organisms to maximize reward and minimize harm.

How these associations are learned and alter behavior across experiences was historically studied using animal conditioning paradigms, where isolated or compound cues were paired with reinforcements or punishments (e.g. Kamin, 1968; Mackintosh, 1975; Rescorla & Wagner, 1972; Pearce & Hall, 1980; Grossberg, 1982).
text.formatted: How these associations are learned and alter behavior across experiences was historically studied using animal conditioning paradigms, where isolated or compound cues were paired with reinforcements or punishments (e.g. <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Kamin, 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Mackintosh, 1975;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">Rescorla & Wagner, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Pearce & Hall, 1980;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Grossberg, 1982)</ref>.

text.text: In several early accounts, attention was described as the latent quantity determining the extent to which credit is assigned to a given cue following an outcome.

Diverging computational theories emerged regarding the relationship between experience and attention allocation. Mackintosh (1975) proposed that attention is allocated to cues that reliably precede the outcome, while others are increasingly ignored.
text.formatted: Diverging computational theories emerged regarding the relationship between experience and attention allocation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">Mackintosh (1975)</ref> proposed that attention is allocated to cues that reliably precede the outcome, while others are increasingly ignored.

text.text: In a model later mirrored by predictive coding in visual perception, Pearce & Hall (1980) proposed that attention decreases alongside increasing prediction accuracy and is maximized when cue-outcome contingencies are uncertain.
text.formatted: In a model later mirrored by predictive coding in visual perception, <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Pearce & Hall (1980)</ref> proposed that attention decreases alongside increasing prediction accuracy and is maximized when cue-outcome contingencies are uncertain.

text.text: While both models suggest that attention serves to maximize accurate predictions, they differ in how attention is purported to achieve this: by focusing on the most predictive cue, or by learning about cues that are least understood (Pearce & Mackintosh, 2010).

text.text: Subsequent hybrid models calculate which cues will be attended based on a combination of associability and prediction error (Pearce et al., 1998; Le Pelley, 2004; Pearce & Mackintosh, 2010; Esber & Haselgrove, 2011).

text.text: This theoretical lineage inspired attention updating models of human category learning, which specify prediction error as a signal to update attention (e.g. Kruschke, 1992; Kruschke & Johansen, 1999; Logan, 2002; Nosofsky et al., 1994; Kruschke, 2003).

text.text: Across these formalizations, attention evolves across trials to balance exploration of uncertain cues with exploitation of reliably diagnostic cues.
In multi-attribute reinforcement learning, selective attention implements a form of feature-based state abstraction.

By weighting task-relevant dimensions and ignoring irrelevant ones, high-dimensional environments can be collapsed into low-dimensional representations (Gershman & Niv, 2010; Wilson & Niv, 2012). Niv et al. (2015) provided relevant insight to this idea by fitting RL models to behavioral data collected while participants chose among stimuli that varied along dimensions of shape, color, and texture.

(2015)</ref> provided relevant insight to this idea by fitting RL models to behavioral data collected while participants chose among stimuli that varied along dimensions of shape, color, and texture.

text.text: Choice behavior was best captured by a model in which associative weights operated at the level of outcomes and individual features and decayed across trials (e.g., a square feature in the shape dimension; f RL + decay) rather than operating on outcomes and feature conjunctions (e.g., a green square with wavy texture).

The degree of feature-value differentiation predicted by f RL + decay tracked BOLD activity in a frontoparietal network consisting of the intraparietal sulcus, precuneus, and dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC), suggesting that this network implements state abstraction based on goal-relevant features.

Because f RL + decay captures choice history without explicit attention parameters, subsequent work investigated when attention operates: Does it weight features during the choice, or does it react to feedback to select which features will contribute to the next choice?

Incorporating fixation data into RL models supported a dual role for attention: attended features were more heavily weighted when calculating stimulus value during the choice, and attention further biased how subjective value was updated during post-feedback credit assignment (Leong et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Incorporating fixation data into RL models supported a dual role for attention: attended features were more heavily weighted when calculating stimulus value during the choice, and attention further biased how subjective value was updated during post-feedback credit assignment <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Leong et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, frontoparietal BOLD activation increased on trials in which prediction errors prompted shifts in gaze, supporting the idea that this network orients attention toward reward-predictive dimensions and reallocates it elsewhere when predictions are violated.
Prediction errors and their influence on attention weights are subject to internal state biases as well (e.g., affect: Bennett et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Prediction errors and their influence on attention weights are subject to internal state biases as well (e.g., affect: <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Bennett et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: While feature-weighting models treat attention as a filter operating over fixed dimensions, attentional selection can also emerge naturally from higher-order belief updating about the structure of the environment.

After learning that different animals occur with different frequencies across sectors of an animal reserve, for example, participants can use a sequence of observed animals to infer which hidden sector most likely generated them.
In Bayesian terms, this hidden context constitutes a latent cause and was found to be represented by the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; Chan et al., 2016).
text.formatted: In Bayesian terms, this hidden context constitutes a latent cause and was found to be represented by the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Chan et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Such belief states could, in turn, provide an overarching con-trol signal for determining which features and past experiences are treated as relevant for ongoing decisions without an explicit attention mechanism.
Although attention is supposedly allocated across features to maximize predictive accuracy, it can, at times, seemingly lead to irrational behaviors.

Two examples are the phenomena of blocking, where a novel cue is ignored when an established cue already predicts the outcome, and highlighting, where a novel cue receives more attention than an established cue when an unpredicted outcome occurs (Kamin, 1968; Medin & Edelson, 1988).
text.formatted: Two examples are the phenomena of blocking, where a novel cue is ignored when an established cue already predicts the outcome, and highlighting, where a novel cue receives more attention than an established cue when an unpredicted outcome occurs <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Kamin, 1968;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Medin & Edelson, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: From a normative statistical standpoint, the "rational" baseline in both cases would be for attention to be proportional to cue validity (i.e., equal attention when both cues are equally predictive of an outcome).
These phenomena provided early evidence that attention does not simply track raw feature-outcome contingencies.

Instead, attention appears to be a resource-rational mechanism that maximizes predictive accuracy within the system's processing constraints (Lieder & Griffiths, 2019). Kruschke et al. (2005) investigated this idea using a connectionist model that implements attention as a finite resource which is updated through error-driven gradient descent.
text.formatted: Instead, attention appears to be a resource-rational mechanism that maximizes predictive accuracy within the system's processing constraints <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(Lieder & Griffiths, 2019)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Kruschke et al. (2005)</ref> investigated this idea using a connectionist model that implements attention as a finite resource which is updated through error-driven gradient descent.

text.text: With these constraints in place, 1) increasing attention toward one cue necessitates decreasing attention toward the others; and 2) attention increases for cues whose contribution reduces error and decreases for misleading cues.

These properties account for blocking and highlighting effects, respectively, whereas model variants without attention constraints predict outcomes strictly in proportion to cue-outcome cooccurrences.
Attention weights predicted by the constrained model additionally mapped onto observed gaze allocation between cues.
While Kruschke et al. (2005) treated attention as a fixedcapacity resource, more recent work formalizes attention allocation as an explicit cost-benefit trade-off (Galdo et al., 2022).
text.formatted: While <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Kruschke et al. (2005)</ref> treated attention as a fixedcapacity resource, more recent work formalizes attention allocation as an explicit cost-benefit trade-off <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Galdo et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The adaptive attention representation model (AARM) updates attention after feedback using an objective function that balances the utility of error reduction against the computational cost of attentional deployment, specifically favoring a sparsity/LASSO (L 1 ) penalty and dimensional competition as proxies for capacity limits.

AARM variants with biases toward minimal attention expenditure provided better fits to choice and dimension-level gaze data across several category learning paradigms than simpler baseline variants in which attention was optimized for error reduction alone.
This progression illustrates that attentional biases are not arbitrarily irrational, but rather emerge as the system attempts to balance predictive accuracy against the cost of resource expenditure.

Translating these algorithmic principles to their neural implementations reveals that attention updating requires coordinated processing instead of being subserved by a single "attention" center. Weichart, Evans, et al. (2022), for example, found that changes in the magnitude of the attention gradient predicted by AARM covaried with BOLD timeseries data across regions canonically involved in category learning (Seger & Miller, 2010).
text.formatted: Translating these algorithmic principles to their neural implementations reveals that attention updating requires coordinated processing instead of being subserved by a single "attention" center. <ref type="bibr" target="#b191">Weichart, Evans, et al. (2022)</ref>, for example, found that changes in the magnitude of the attention gradient predicted by AARM covaried with BOLD timeseries data across regions canonically involved in category learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">(Seger & Miller, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This network spans parietal cortex (orienting), visual cortex (visual perception), hippocampus and medial temporal lobe (retrieval of previously-stored objects), midbrain and basal ganglia (prediction error), and PFC (goal maintenance).

This finding suggests that error-and cost-driven attentional tuning alters processing from end-toend: from the perceptual acquisition of features, to the biased representation of objects, to the overarching decision policy.
A core hub within this network is the loop between the PFC and hippocampus, which dynamically reorganizes stored representations as task demands shift.

In a modelbased fMRI analysis using the category learning model, SUSTAIN (Love et al., 2004), functional coupling between PFC and hippocampus was shown to track modelpredicted shifts in object similarity when task demands change (Mack et al., 2016).

text.text: The authors compared patients with focal dlPFC or vmPFC lesions and healthy controls across unidimensional rule-based (RB), multidimensional informationintegration (II), and category learning tasks.

Consistent with their specialized roles, dlPFC damage primarily impaired performance on perceptual discrimination tasks (RB and II), whereas vmPFC damage primarily disrupted category learning, where success depended on identifying a deterministic dimension amid probabilistic distractors.
Comparisons of fitted AARM parameters showed that damage to either subregion increased attention regularization, reflecting a general tendency to rely on fewer dimensions compared to controls.
Initial values of the model's latent attention variable primarily accounted for performance differences between lesion groups.

One explanation for the latter finding is that the authors' model specification assumes low-level perceptual discrim-inability and higher-level construction of a decision variable are controlled by the same variable.

Initialized values may have been the only available knob for capturing reduced perceptual discriminability among dlPFC patients and reduced ability to discriminate between dimensions in terms of predictive value among vmPFC patients.

text.text: While attention in learning is often formalized as latent weights distributed over stimulus dimensions, observers deploy attention as an active information sampling policy that is expressed through sequential fixations.
Framing attention weights as an information sampling policy connects two complementary domains.
In category learning, these policies determine how learned dimension priorities generate withintrial fixation sequences across features before committing to a choice.
In value-based decision-making, gaze operates as an optimal sampling policy that balances uncertainty reduction against time costs.

Although changes in attention weights across learning may be reflected in proportions of fixations across dimensions (Rehder & Hoffman, 2005a), learning models are not typically explicit about how expectations about dimension relevance translate into information sampling behaviors.

text.text: One way to bridge learned attention weights with feature sampling is by mirroring the mechanics that control post-feedback attention updates into within-trial sampling dynamics (Weichart, Galdo, et al., 2022).

text.text: When a stimulus is presented, AARM's within-trial module utilizes attention weights to probabilistically select a dimension to fixate first.
As the feature in the fixated dimension is encoded, matching exemplars are stochastically activated in memory.
Those activations are converted to decision variables corresponding to the available category responses (Nosofsky, 1986).
text.formatted: Those activations are converted to decision variables corresponding to the available category responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">(Nosofsky, 1986)</ref>.

text.text: If the difference in response activation exceeds a decision threshold, no further dimensions are fixated and a response is made (as in evidence accumulation models).
Otherwise, attention is updated within-trial to maximize the probability of responding consistently with the currently-leading option, and a new dimension is fixated.
In another account, dimensions are selected for fixation based on predicted information gain (Braunlich & Love, 2022).
text.formatted: In another account, dimensions are selected for fixation based on predicted information gain <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Braunlich & Love, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The Sampling Emergent Attention (SEA) model assumes that the representational feature space is partitioned into clusters, and the observer can estimate the probability that a new item belongs to each available cluster given the observation of one or more features.
The expected utility of observing each possible feature informs which dimension to sample.
Attention is thus formalized as the expected gain in utility from sampling each dimension.
A third account selects dimensions to sample by combining influences across three modularized control units (Lag-1; Barnes et al., 2022).
text.formatted: A third account selects dimensions to sample by combining influences across three modularized control units (Lag-1; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Barnes et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: On each trial, stimulus features are represented as spatially locked inputs to a visual field.
Competition in a spatial attention field yields a prioritized fixation target, and saccades are initiated when activity in a motor field crosses a threshold.
Feature information extracted at each fixation activates feature detectors and category nodes.
As evidence accumulates during a trial, the system dynamically reorients gaze toward additional diagnostic features until a category response threshold is reached.

While attention in these three models serves the objective of acquiring information that will maximize the probability of a correct response, they instantiate it in different ways: Weichart, Galdo, et al. (2022) by first reading out learned attention weights and then biasing sampling toward the leading hypothesis, Braunlich & Love (2022) by simulating all possible sampling sequences and enacting the one with the best expected outcome, and Barnes et al. (2022) through a dynamical priority map that is continuously shaped by expected gain.

text.text: In value-based choice, information sampling can be formalized as an optimal control problem in which attention balances uncertainty reduction against sampling costs, such as dwell duration and saccade transitions (F. Callaway et al., 2021; Shimojo et al., 2003; Gluth et al., 2020).

text.text: Under this framework, gaze allocation is determined by a combination of estimated uncertainty about the value of each option relative to competing alternatives.
Whereas standard gazeinfused decision-making accounts treat attention as a filter that biases evidence accumulation (e.g.

Krajbich, 2019), framing attention as a control policy demonstrates how topdown mechanisms actively determine which options are inspected and for how long to efficiently reduce uncertainty before a choice.
This active sampling perspective extends beyond uncertainty reduction to encompass goal-dependent prioritization.

Observers preferentially sample high-value items during ap-proach decisions (selecting a preferred option) but reallocate fixations toward low-value items during avoidance decisions (rejecting an undesirable option; Sepulveda et al., 2020).

text.text: By approaching attention through the lens of the computational problem it solves (i.e. maximizing goalconsistent responses, reducing uncertainty, and minimizing time), these approaches redress a longstanding issue in the broader attention-mediated decision-making literature.
Knowing that fixations guide choices offers little inferential value if we do not have a complete understanding of what drives the sampling process in the first place.
The broad and heterogeneous use of the term "attention" has long complicated attempts to explain conceptually-linked phenomena from a mechanistic standpoint.

Invoking "attention" as a latent explanans for such phenomena provides limited explanatory power (Hommel et al., 2019), yet neural or mathematical explication of any single phenomenon cannot be expected to generalize across them all (Allport, 1993).

text.text: One solution is to allow that "attentional" phenomena arise from multiple distinguishable processes-a perspective with which the current review aligns-and, more generally, to replace appeals to "attention" as an explanatory cause with explicit accounts of the mechanisms that produce the phenomena of interest (Di Lollo, 2018).

text.text: Model-based cognitive neuroscience implements this strategy by mathematically specifying mechanisms for "attention" and adjudicating between competing hypotheses based on their ability to account for observed behavior, often while constrained by process-level data.

However, a new problem has arguably arisen whereby mechanisms are highly contextualized by the modeling frameworks in which they were embedded and the paradigms those frameworks were developed to accommodate.
Individual papers often tell us what a mechanism does within this model and this task, while providing little sense of which aspects retain theoretical significance outside of that context.

This review operates at a higher level of abstraction than specific algorithms and neural implementations (Marr, 1982), while preserving the notion that "attention" should be understood as multiple mechanisms.

text.text: Organizing the target literature based on the computational-level functions that "attention" serves across multiple contexts has proven revealing in several respects.
First, similar algorithmic motifs do not imply shared processes.

Algorithms for multiplicative enhancement, for example, appear in models of perceptual encoding, memory gating, and value-based evidence accumulation, despite loading on different neurophysiological measures and serving different computational functions.
Replacing the term "attention" with a collection of operational definitions risks reproducing the same explanatory problem at a lower level of description.
Second, while mechanisms for attention are often studied at bounded timescales, this does not imply that mechanisms operate independently between timescales.

Models of value-based decision-making, for example, may query or freely-estimate an option's subjective value and implement "attention" as a regulator of evidence accumulation relative to an alternative.
The subjective values that enter this process, however, reflect the culmination of experiences over a longer timescale, which may themselves have been shaped by selective information processing.
Likewise, biases expressed during a single choice can determine what information is sampled and available in future contexts.
Third, algorithmic dissimilarity does not imply computational dissimilarity.
In many examples provided in this review, multiple algorithms account for the same phenomenon or achieve a similar functional outcome.

Considered only at the algorithmic level, these accounts may appear fundamentally distinct; considered at the computational level, they can instead be understood as alternative implementations of a common functional solution.
This distinction helps localize theoretical disagreement.
Competing accounts may disagree about how a function is realized without disagreeing about what function is being served.
The functional correspondences identified here can motivate hypotheses about relations among mechanisms without implying that those mechanisms instantiate a common process.

Recent proposals for relational definitions provide one framework for evaluating such hypotheses. Kvam & Alaukik (2026), for example, framed relational definitions around the question of whether parameters or measures that are taken to reflect the same theoretical construct exhibit shared structure across tasks.

text.text: The present synthesis suggests a complementary basis for generating such tests.

Whereas relational approaches may begin with parameters or measures conventionally assigned to the same construct, the present framework suggests that computational function can provide another theoretically motivated basis for identifying processes whose relationships are worth testing.

Thus, two task-specific processes need not both instantiate "competition," "gain," or another common algorithmic motif to motivate a relational hypothesis; their shared functional role may itself provide a theoretically meaningful basis for asking whether they covary or generalize across contexts.
Several caveats apply to the organizing framework presented here.
First, the objective-constraint structure is partly interpretive.

Not all of the reviewed studies explicitly characterize "attention" in terms of an objective to be achieved under processing constraints, although many formalize mechanisms in ways that permit such an interpretation and some modeling traditions are explicitly grounded in performance tradeoffs (e.g., EAMs).
Second, the proposed solutions are necessarily provisional because they were derived from a restricted subset of the literature.

Our inclusion criteria favored computational accounts constrained by neurophysio-logical or neuroanatomical data, excluding relevant phenomena and modeling traditions that have not been studied using these approaches.
Inclusion should therefore not be interpreted as a judgment of theoretical importance, nor should the resulting framing be considered exhaustive.
Additional modeling traditions may reveal further solutions, alter the boundaries among those identified here, or expose distinctions that are not apparent in the present sample.
Finally, mechanistic conclusions drawn from model comparison remain conditional on the hypothesis space considered.
A bestfitting model identifies the most successful account among the alternatives tested, but cannot establish that its assumptions uniquely characterize the true data-generating process.
These limitations bound the claims of the present synthesis while preserving its utility as a framework for organizing formally specified accounts of attentional phenomena.
This function-first organization preserves the mechanistic diversity of "attention" while providing a common level of analysis across otherwise siloed modeling traditions.
Advancing cumulative theory may require moving beyond asking what "attention" is, and instead asking what the multiple mechanisms described as "attention" do.
